narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 63.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty, but it is high enough that the admissions process treated the risk as too great.

The strongest factor was your family-income background. Compared with admitted students, who were most often upper-middle income, your middle-income bracket was the single largest push toward the failure prediction. The next strongest factor was your first-year class standing: your decile of 5 was below the admitted-student average of 6, and that lower early academic position also pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 39 was above the admitted-student average of 37.18, but it carried less weight and, in your overall profile, still leaned toward the failure side rather than offsetting the other factors. Your third-year decile, undergraduate GPA, gender, race, and full-time status were not among the top three influences in this decision.

To respond, ask the admissions office for a formal review and whether a bar-readiness plan, academic advising, or additional coursework could address the concerns. If reapplying, focus on strengthening your first-year academic record or explaining any circumstances behind it, and ask whether a higher LSAT or a targeted study plan would change the assessment.
